details:
**Hiding in the Heavenly Rock Cave**
After her brother Susanoo's rampage through heaven, Amaterasu shuts herself inside the cave Ama-no-Iwato, plunging the world into darkness. This is the most famous story about the Shinto sun goddess and appears in nearly every question.

**Flayed horse thrown into her weaving hall**
Susanoo's worst offense is hurling a flayed (skinned) horse, often described as a dappled pony, through the roof of Amaterasu's sacred weaving hall. One of her weaving maidens is killed by a shuttle in the chaos, and Amaterasu retreats into the cave. He also defiles her rice fields and halls, including with feces.

**Uzume's dance**
To lure Amaterasu out, the goddess Ame-no-Uzume performs a wild, bawdy dance on an overturned tub, exposing herself and making the assembled gods roar with laughter. Curious about the noise, Amaterasu peeks out.

**Yata no Kagami (the sacred mirror)**
The gods hang a mirror and jewels on a sacred tree outside the cave. When Amaterasu sees her own dazzling reflection, she steps out, and the strong god Ame-no-Tajikarao pulls her the rest of the way so light returns. This mirror became one of the Imperial Regalia and is said to be kept at the Ise Shrine.

**Born from Izanagi's left eye**
After returning from the underworld Yomi, the creator god Izanagi purifies himself by washing. Amaterasu is born from his left eye, the moon god Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and the storm god Susanoo from his nose. Together they are called the Three Precious Children, and Amaterasu is given rule over the High Plain of Heaven (Takamagahara).

**Ninigi and the Three Sacred Treasures**
Amaterasu sends her grandson Ninigi down from heaven to rule the earth, giving him the mirror Yata no Kagami, the jewel Yasakani no Magatama, and the sword Kusanagi. These became the Imperial Regalia of Japan.

**Descent of the imperial family**
Japan's emperors, who sit on the Chrysanthemum Throne, traditionally claim descent from Amaterasu through Ninigi; Ninigi's great-grandson is the first emperor, Jimmu. Emperors continued to invoke this descent even after Emperor Hirohito's 1946 Humanity Declaration renounced imperial divinity.

**Sword-chewing contest with Susanoo**
To test whether Susanoo's intentions are pure, the siblings hold a contest of producing children. Amaterasu breaks Susanoo's sword into pieces, chews them, and spits out three goddesses, while Susanoo chews her jewels or necklace and produces five male gods.

**Ise Grand Shrine**
Amaterasu's chief shrine is the Inner Shrine (Naiku) at Ise, founded according to tradition by the princess Yamatohime. It is ritually torn down and rebuilt every twenty years, and an imperial princess called the saio once served there as priestess.

**Killing of the food goddess**
In one version, the moon god Tsukuyomi kills the food goddess Uke Mochi after she produces food from her mouth, nose, and rear. Disgusted, Amaterasu refuses ever to see him again, which explains why the sun and moon are never in the sky together and the separation of day and night. In the Kojiki, Susanoo kills a similar food goddess, Ogetsu-hime.

**Kusanagi**
The "grass-cutting" sword that Susanoo finds inside a tail of the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi. He presents it to Amaterasu to reconcile with her, and she later passes it to Ninigi.

**Ninigi's marriage**
Ninigi chooses to marry Konohanasakuya-hime, the princess of blossoms, and rejects her sister Iwanaga-hime, the princess of rocks. As a result, he and his descendants, the emperors, become short-lived like flowers instead of enduring like stone.

**Yatagarasu**
A three-legged crow that serves as Amaterasu's messenger and, in legend, guides Emperor Jimmu through the mountains during his conquest.

**Shinmei and Tensho Daijin**
Alternate names for Amaterasu. Shinmei shrines dedicated to her form a network modeled on Ise, and Tensho Daijin is the Sino-Japanese reading of her title.

**Origin of rice and silkworms**
From the body of the slain food goddess came rice, grains, and silkworms. Amaterasu planted the seeds in the fields of heaven and placed the silkworms in her mouth to draw silk thread, establishing agriculture and sericulture (silk farming).
